Sauver Noël, un repas à la fois: Saving Christmas, One Meal at a Time
Chaque année, ils sont nombreux à s’impl: Every year, many people get involved in organizing the Christmas dinner.
Le NDG Christmas Dinner, un dîner de Noë: The NDG Christmas Dinner has been held in Notre-Dame-de-Grâce for some forty years.
On pourrait dire que Paul Shubin est un: You could say Paul Shubin is an emblematic figure of the neighbourhood. With good reason: for more than 25 years, he has organized the NDG Christmas Dinner, which has been held in Notre-Dame-de-Grâce for some forty years. Despite his legendary affability, the endearing Mr. Shubin refuses to have his photo taken. He is truly unpretentious. “There's no meeting, no boss, no organization, nothing,” he says. The event is spectacular and puts everyone on an equal footing. Because of COVID-19, the last edition of the dinner took place on December 25, 2019. On that occasion, 1,100 meals were served in the hall of St. Ignatius of Loyola Church.
Ici, on ne compte pas. Les convives sont: Here, nobody's counting. Guests are seated and served without having to justify their presence. “It's a major event in Notre-Dame-de-Grâce,” says Mr. Shubin of the dinner, which is funded by donations from the community. Legend has it that the dinner has been around for 40 years, but in reality there is no official record of the first editions.
« Et si vous voyiez la composition démog: “And if you saw the demographic makeup of the guests, you'd realize it's not meant for any one person in particular, it's for everybody,” he adds. Everyone who wants to and is able to come is welcome, as Mr. Shubin explains, mentioning seniors, people who don't feel like cooking, single people, families and people living in precarious situations. “We don't ask any questions, we don't ask who needs it.” Children are welcome too, and gifts are waiting for them.
« En réalité, le père Noël est juif », d: “Actually, Santa Claus is Jewish,” says Mr. Shubin, who himself celebrates both Hanukkah and Christmas with his family. About 27 years ago – Mr. Shubin isn't sure – he found himself helping with the Christmas dinner for the first time, after some volunteers dropped out at the last minute. “And my late wife, I don't remember why, said she was going to take it over. She dragged me into the kitchen,” he recalls. Over time, he decided to do more, and it has now been going on for nearly 30 years. His own children, who are now in their thirties and live a few steps from Mr. Shubin's home, grew up revolving around the event.
« Mes enfants allaient jouer avec les au: “My kids would go play with the other kids,” he says. When they were old enough, they went to help in the kitchen. The eldest, James, is now in charge of a legendary sauce, which he makes himself on site.
Chaque année, ils sont nombreux à s’impl: Every year, many people get involved in organizing the Christmas dinner. First, volunteers offer to cook a turkey, which they bring to the church on December 24. The turkeys are carved there, while the rest of the feast – stuffing, mashed potatoes, vegetables and gravy – is cooked on site at St. Ignatius Church by about ten cooks at the stoves. Up to 50 volunteers take care of the food so that everyone is warmly welcomed on December 25 at 1 p.m. Listening to him, you get the impression that organizing such a celebration is a walk in the park. “One day in November, I don't really know when, I tell myself it's time to call the tithe givers,” he explains. Sometimes they are waiting for his call with a certain impatience: Mr. Shubin hadn't realized he was late. “And then somebody starts calling the volunteers. But it's totally organic. I don't know if that's the right word. It kind of happens on its own, in a way.”
<strong>‍</strong>En 2020, pour la premi: ‍In 2020, for the first time, the event had to be cancelled because physical distancing could not be respected. But it was only postponed since the 2021 edition, despite major adjustments, was expected to go ahead. “We said to ourselves that we had to do something. We're limited, though. We could easily have not done it, but that's not our style,” Mr. Shubin continues. This year, the dinner's volunteers planned to hand out 150 takeout meals. “Because there's no way to have an army of people peeling and chopping vegetables, we're going to cheat with a giveaway,” he says of the idea, which was suggested by a friend who volunteers for the event and is a chef by profession.
Dans la cuisine de sa maison centenaire,: In the kitchen of his century-old home, where he has lived for 38 years, Mr. Shubin was getting ready with his partners in crime to pack up the meals on December 25. The food, cooked in advance, promises to be just as delicious, our head cook assures us. With COVID-19 cases on the rise, the plans have just changed. Since people can't gather, the whole turkeys and sides prepared by the volunteers will be given to families by the NDG Community Council, a local non-profit organization, which will handle the distribution on December 25. “It's none of our business to investigate people's personal needs. We're here to serve a meal, whatever the situation,” says Mr. Shubin. Every year, the leftovers are brought to Mission Bon Accueil on December 26.
Comme chaque fois, aucune nourriture ne: As always, no food will be wasted. During our meeting, Mr. Shubin's landline and cellphone ring several times. It's the cooks, giving and getting updates. Paul Shubin hopes the Christmas dinner can come back to life next year in its original form. “It's a lot of fun, and it keeps me young,” he says. “I love it, I've been an event coordinator all my life,” confides the man, who has also been a writer, translator and editor. The rest of the year, Mr. Shubin doesn't seem to get too bored. “I made a ton of spaghetti sauce this fall. I got carried away, I made 42 jars!
Je me suis promené dans la rue pour en d: I walked up and down the street giving it to the neighbours,” he says. The same thing happened with canned vegetables and applesauce. “I can't eat all that!” says the man, who has lived alone since his wife died of cancer last January. Why make so much, we ask him. “Because it's fun to make it and to give it away.”
